Joost believes he can make oil from dirty plastic

Experts scoff but Joost believes he can make oil from dirty plastic

By Liam Mannix July 14, 2019 — 4.02pm • Share on Facebook • Share on Twitter • Send via Email Normal text sizeLarger text sizeVery large text size 6 View all comments Inside the old jam factory in Monbulk, just down the road from his organic farm, environmentalist Joost Bakker has built what he hopes could be part of the solution to Australia’s recycling crisis. It’s a multimillion-dollar pyrolysis plant, funded by local investors. Mr Bakker believes it is the first plant of its type in Australia.

The pyrolisis plant at Monbulk.CREDIT:JASON SOUTH You put contaminated plastic waste in one end, cook it at about 200 degrees and collect the crude oil that comes out the other end. The oil can then be refined and used as petrol. “The only other thing you end up with is carbon. The carbon can go into steel, it can go into tyres, or ink,” says Mr Bakker. “There is no waste.” Advertisement RELATED ARTICLE

INDONESIA Deal with your own 'toxic' waste, says Jakarta Add to shortlist Mr Bakker hopes this plant can help deal with the rising amount of plastic piling up across the country since China banned recycling imports in 2018. This month Indonesia sent back an Australian shipping container packed full of contaminated plastic recycling. But the dream of turning rubbish into liquid gold has entranced many entrepreneurs over the years, and there are almost as many proposed pyrolysis plants as there are failed ones. Scientists and conservationists are sceptical. “Pyrolysis is not a new technology,” says Adam Lee, a professor of sustainable chemistry.“This sounds too good to be true.” Mr Bakker first found fame as a florist for top restaurants but is now better known as an eco-entrepreneur with a green finger in many sustainable ventures. He founded several (now closed) zero-waste restaurants, as well as proposing an eco-housing development that fell over amid delays and rising costs. The pyrolysis plant has always been a dream of his. He’d prefer the world did not generate any waste, he says. “But I came to realise that it’s not going to happen." Pyrolysis is his solution. Clean plastic can easily be recycled. But "contaminated plastic", the mix of different plastics and food waste that comes out of household recycling bins, is much harder and more expensive. “That’s why it’s sent to third-world countries – because you can pay someone $2 [a day] to take the bottletops off milk bottles,” Mr Bakker says.

Contaminated plastic waiting to go into the plant.CREDIT:JASON SOUTH His pilot plant happily accepts nearly all types of plastic mixed together, turning 10 tonnes of plastic into about 8000 litres of oil. He hopes to prove the technology and then sell it to local councils. But pyrolysis comes with inherent problems. First, the oil that comes out is only as pure as the plastic you put in. Contaminated plastic produces low-grade oil, which has to be further blended or refined before it can be used. “It’s better than doing nothing. But it’s more complex than suggesting you can throw in any old mix of waste plastics and get out a useable fuel oil,” says Professor Lee, who researches pyrolysis at RMIT.

Crude oil sits in drums after being produced by the plant.CREDIT:JASON SOUTH Mr Bakker claims his oil is so pure that his business partner has been running his LandCruiser off it. The process also produces gases which can be toxic. Mr Bakker says his technology, imported from Korea, captures all those gases and reuses them. But a proposed pyrolysis plant in Hume, ACT, was canned after locals objected to potential health risks. The plants only make money when the price of crude oil is high. “If the oil price drops, anyone trying to do this automatically cannot make a profit,” says Professor Lee. Mr Bakker admits the plant would cost more to run than it would earn. He did not yet have final costings, he said.

Joost Bakker with tulips, on his farm in Monbulk last year.CREDIT: PAUL JEFFERS And the environmental benefits are not clear-cut. The pyrolysis machine burns diesel to melt the plastic. And the oil you get at the end is also destined to be eventually burnt, releasing greenhouse gases. “If you’re going to burn it in the end, you’re still going to add carbon to the atmosphere,” says Jono La Nauze, chief executive of Environment Victoria. “That’s not recycling.”
